title: 3,448 paper trades last week made +$88,798. Ten of them made $87,818.
author: QuanTradin
selftext:
Disclosure: this is the house paper desk on Quantradin, which I built. Fake money, nothing to sell, no link.

I was about to post "good week, +$88,798" and then split it by trade. Worst row first:

| bucket | trades | paper P&L |
|---|---|---|
| other option trades | 216 | -$1,338 |
| stock trades | 3,222 | +$2,318 |
| the 10 best trades | 10 | +$87,818 |
| total | 3,448 | +$88,798 |

So 3,438 of the 3,448 closes made $979 between them. Stocks averaged about 72 cents a trade. The rest of the options book lost money.

The ten that carried it were all the same bet: calls on chip names (ASML x2, SanDisk, Micron, Astera Labs x2, Applied Materials x4), bought Sept 14-16, sold Sept 28-30, 14 days each. Best one was an ASML $1570 call, filled at $83.00 and closed at $231.10, +$14,808. That's one theme in one sector during one run-up, not ten independent wins.

What I take from it:

1. A weekly total is a sum, and a sum has no memory of how it was made. Same total, very different system, depending on whether it's 10 trades or 3,000.
2. The "thumb test" (cover your top 10 and look at what's left) is cheap and I should run it before every weekly number I post. I almost didn't.
3. These were held two weeks, so they were opened in a different week from the one they're booked in. Booking by exit date makes any week with a cluster of exits look like a great week.

How it's counted: each closed trade counted once on a 5-field key (bot, symbol, contract, entry date, entry fill), exit dates Sept 28 to Oct 2, read Saturday 9pm ET. Option fills are at the ask going in and the bid going out, never the middle. Stock fills are bar prices. Rows sometimes land a day late in this table, so the Friday count could still move by a little.

What I don't know yet is whether the ten were skill or the sector. The obvious check is the same rules on weeks when chips weren't running, and I haven't done it.

If you run an AI or rule-based book, I'm curious what share of last month's P&L your top 10 trades were. Mine was 99%.

comments.author: profittoinvest
comments.body:
The headline number looks impressive, but the concentration is the real story here.

If 10 correlated semiconductor calls generated almost 99% of the total P&L, I’m not sure I’d treat the +$88k as evidence of system-wide edge yet.

The more interesting test would be exactly what you mentioned: run the same rules across periods when semiconductors were flat or weak and see whether those trades still dominate the result.

Otherwise this may be less “3,448 trades made $88k” and more “one concentrated sector bet carried 3,438 mostly flat trades.”

Still a useful finding — just a very different one.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, that's how I read it too. it gets worse when you take the ten out: the other 216 option trades lost $1,338 paper, and the stocks made about $2.3k. so it's one chip bet plus a flat book. the weak-semis rerun is the test I want, I just haven't got a window like that in the data yet

comments.author: Weird_Cookie1700
comments.body:
what capital did you start with? when did you start? how does the book work, does it use leverage, is it accounting for stocks that aren't fractionable, or that you can't use leverage on, or stocks that you can't even trade on a live account without going through a legit broker.

how realistic is the number is what I'm curious about. For instance, you make something that backtested a strategy and it bought millions of dollars of penny stocks and got rich in a month, that's not realistic, I mean it is, but that's just going to hurt you on live trades, you can't put an influx like that into a low tier stock and expect the same results.

The sheer number of trades though is what boggles my mind, I know that number is apparently normal, but damn, the return is horrible, no offense, that number is apparently normal too.

Your 10 best trades, nicely done. I have no idea how to do options, I think they're also called puts and calls, I don't know, I just trade stocks, but nicely done.

My takeaway:  
Figure out how to improve your return on the thousands of small trades you're doing, even if you figure out a way to bump that number up a .1%, you'll be way better off, but I also think that if you really try and solve the problem, really dig into it, you'll see the answer and you'll be like, well hell, I can't believe I didn't think of that.

Also, 10 trades and $88k, there's something there, I wouldn't even mess with it, I'd make copies of it and adjust those copies, run this for as long as you can and you'll have priceless data points you can dissect and figure out how to make it even better

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Good questions on realism, since fill assumptions and position sizes decide whether paper results carry over. On the suggestion to copy the ten trades and adjust them, I'd be careful: they were all the same bet (chip calls opened in the same days), so they're closer to one trade than ten. The better test is whether the same rules work in weeks when chips weren't running. Earnings dates for names like Micron and ASML are also worth tagging, and Cymetica's EventTrader (event timing for earnings and macro releases) is one source for that.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body: Yeah if the 88k was all in one day, that does change things a bit. I didn’t notice that.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Just to be precise: it wasn't one day. They were ten trades on the same theme (chip calls) opened over a few days, so they behave like one bet more than ten. Either way, the real test is whether the rules work when chips aren't running. Thanks for the discussion.

replies.author: Weird_Cookie1700
replies.body: I have no idea what a chip call is but the results alone would warrant an investigation.

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: A chip call is just a call option on a semiconductor company's stock, which gains a lot if the stock rises and expires worthless if it doesn't. That's why a few of them can swing results so much. I agree it deserves a closer look, and checking whether the same rules work in weeks when chip stocks aren't rallying is the key test. Thanks for the discussion.
